Cells going through meiosis must divide twice to achieve two key goals:

1. **Reduce chromosome number by half:**  
   The first division, called **Meiosis I**, separates homologous chromosomes (pairs of similar chromosomes, one from each parent). This reduces the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n), meaning the daughter cells have only one set of chromosomes instead of two.

2. **Separate sister chromatids:**  
   The second division, called **Meiosis II**, is similar to mitosis. It separates the sister chromatids of each chromosome into different cells. This ensures that each haploid daughter cell has just one copy of each chromosome.

Together, these two divisions ensure that gametes (sperm or eggs) have half the usual number of chromosomes, so that when fertilization occurs, the resulting offspring have the correct diploid chromosome number. Without two divisions, chromosome number would not be properly halved, leading to cells with too many chromosomes.
